newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions see no point in new talks on jobs.
newsitem.headline: German unions see no point in new talks on jobs.

text.p: German labour union leaders said on Tuesday they saw no point in holding fresh talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl on joint efforts to halve unemployment.

One year after a landmark meeting on the Alliance for Jobs, labour leaders are resisting calls from government and business for renewed top-level talks. They say their initial concepts have been twisted and there have been few concrete results.

Klaus Zwickel, head of Germany's largest labour union IG Metall and the initiator of the Alliance for Jobs idea, said he was equally frustrated with a series of sector-specific talks on improving investment conditions in Germany.

"We have had no shortage of talks. What is needed is initiative. There has been almost nothing in the way of concrete results," Zwickel told journalists. "The last talks (with Kohl) failed, and not because of us."

Roland Issen, chairman of the DAG civil servants' union, said, "There is no change in the goal of halving unemployment, but the government's Action Programme for More Jobs and Growth has had no positive impact on the jobs market.
He and other labour leaders say the government programme unveiled last spring emphasized employers' aims of cutting taxes and labour costs, and did little to help job security.
"On the contrary, unemployment has grown drastically," Issen added. German unemployment climbed to a postwar record of over 4.1 million in December and appears to be heading higher.
One of the most prominent government steps was to allow companies greater freedom to reduce sick pay. But later agreements led to restoration of full sick pay in many cases.
Zwickel and Issen participated on Tuesday in talks with Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt on how to promote jobs in the electronics industry.
Rexrodt defended last year's talks with Kohl, saying discussions have a value in themselves, even if solutions appear distant.
"Our society, our citizens expect it of us," Rexrodt said. "I think this discussion has not been brought to a satisfactory end, and it deserves to be."

Sectoral talks on the auto, steel and other industries have focused on their specific problems. Many other sectors, including chemicals, textiles, services, construction and tourism are anxious to hold similar talks, Rexrodt said.
